paper_title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: -05-X-03), Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, and exploitation sightings. We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence Cedric Bonhomme Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg (CIRCL) cedric.bonhomme@circl.lu [57B7 A70D] Alexandre Dulaunoy Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg (CIRCL) alexandre.dulaunoy@circl.lu [44E6 CBCD] 17 November 2026 Submitted to the FIRST.org 2027 Cyber Threat Intelligence Conference, Berlin, Germany Abstract How long are vulnerabilities exploited before fix is available? We compute, for each vulnerability, the interval between exploitation and patch, and lifecycle intervals adapted from the Vulnerability Timeline and Exposure Metrics framework (VTEM), from open, machine-readable evidence: CVE and CSAF records, publisher timelines (GCVE BCP-05-X-03), several Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogs and sightings. An evidence model selects the earliest evidence of each lifecycle event, uses only records that describe the vulnerability itself, carries the precision of every date and traces each figure to the record that produced it; it is implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup. Over the 3,758 identifiers with exploitation evidence on one instance, disclosure is dated for 98%, patch evidence exists for 15.7%, and the vendor-side dates VTEM requires are never published. Most exploitation dates are catalog listings, 1,041 of them on days catalog listed or imported backlog. Setting those and unordered same-day pairs aside, 59 vulnerabilities have patch evidence after exploitation evidence, by median of 7.6 days, mostly from catalog listing to distributors fix. Traceability made the data correctable: one collector recorded exploit publications as exploitation, 40% of the exploitation dates of first measurement, and one catalog dated 11% of its listings with the vulnerabilitys publication time. The intervals can be computed; what limits them is the evidence publishers release, and we identify the timeline, observation and fix dates that would close the gap.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: When vulnerability is exploited, the question that matters to defender is whether fix existed, and if not, for how long the exploitation ran before one did. The question is old. Arbaugh et al. proposed life-cycle model of vulnerabilities [1]; Frei et al. measured the gap between exploit and patch availability [10, 11]; Bilge and Dumitras found zero-day attacks lasting 312 days on average before disclosure [2]. Each answer rests on the data its authors could assemble (public vulnerability databases, vendors telemetry, threat intelligence teams tracking) and is reported mainly as aggregates. Aggregates are fragile: Householder et al. found median time to exploit publication of 2 days but mean of 91 days [14]. Here we report per-vulnerability intervals with machine-readable provenance alongside the aggregates. In 2015, the Vulnerability Timeline and Exposure Metrics framework (VTEM) [17] named the dates of vulnerabilitys lifecycle and the metrics computed from them, and observed that vendors and coordinators seldom publish those dates. Since then the dates have started to appear in machine-readable form: CVE records carry publication and 1 disclosure dates [19], CSAF advisories carry dated vendor fixes [18], several catalogs list known exploited vulnerabilities with dates [8], sightings record observations of exploitation and of public proofs of concept, and GCVEs BCP-05X-03 extension lets publisher put the whole handling timeline in the record [9, 12]. This paper asks how far that open evidence gets today: for how many exploited vulnerabilities the interval between exploitation and patch can be computed, from what kind of evidence, and with what confidence. We make four contributions. 1. An evidence model that computes, per vulnerability, the interval between exploitation and patch and intervals adapted from those VTEM names, from typed evidence only. It selects the earliest evidence of each event, uses only records that state that they describe the vulnerability, carries the precision of every date into bounds and an explicit order, and keeps the source of every figure (Tables 1 and 3). 2. Its reference implementation in VulnerabilityLookup [6, 3], where every vulnerability page and the timeline API show the intervals with their evidence. 3. measurement over the 3,758 identifiers with exploitation evidence on one instance: coverage of each lifecycle event, the kind of date behind each exploitation anchor, and the intervals, split by sign and with catalog backlogs and unordered pairs set aside. based forecasts in exploratory tests [4], motivating sourceexclusion checks here. Here we combine typed inputs from several open sources, distinguish exploitation from exploit publication, and keep per-vulnerability provenance to measure evidence coverage. 4. Corrections of the evidence that the traceability of the model exposed, one of which had turned 40% of the exploitation dates into exploit publication dates, and the publisher-side changes that would close the remaining gaps.

sections.title: 2 Background and Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Vulnerability lifecycle models Arbaugh, Fithen and McHugh proposed life-cycle model for system vulnerabilities and applied it to three case studies [1]. Frei et al. measured discovery, disclosure, exploit and patch dates at scale [10], and later used about 27,000 vulnerabilities disclosed over decade to quantify the systematic gap between exploit and patch availability, together with metric for the success of responsible disclosure [11]. The Vulnerability Timeline and Exposure Metrics framework (VTEM) [17] names nine lifecycle dates (introduced, discovered, vendor informed, vendor acknowledged, vendor solution, disclosure, third-party solution, exploit published and solution implemented) and derives metrics from them: vendor response time (acknowledgement minus notification), time to patch (solution minus notification), total time to patch (solution minus discovery), and an organisations time of exposure (implementation minus solution). Its purpose is the evaluation of vendors and products and of an organisations own exposure, through roll-ups over the vulnerabilities of product or vendor. Its authors illustrated it on vulnerabilities whose dates they knew first-hand, and observed that vendors and coordinators seldom publish such dates. 2.2 Measured intervals Bilge and Dumitras identified 18 vulnerabilities exploited before their disclosure in telemetry from 11 million hosts; the attacks lasted between 19 days and 30 months, 312 days on average, and the volume of attacks rose by up to five orders of magnitude once the vulnerabilities were disclosed [2]. Householder et al. studied 75,807 CVE identifiers, of which 3,164 had public exploit code: the median time to exploit publication was 2 days but the mean 91 days, contrast that recurs whenever these intervals are summarised [14]. Charrier and Weiner tracked 138 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2023 and exploited in the wild, 97 of them as zero-days, and report an average time to exploit of five days; they note that their figures are conservative because first-exploitation dates are rarely published, or only to the month or quarter [5]. Li and Paxson examined the development of security patches at scale [15]. Bonhomme and Dulaunoy found SARIMAX unstable on sparse, bursty sightings, with more stable count2.3 Machine-readable sources CVE records [19] carry publication, reservation, update and optional public-disclosure dates. CVE and NVD references have URLs and tags but no dates [7]: patch tag does not date release. Version-status entries in affected are undated; the optional timeline is free text without event types. CSAF 2.0 advisories [18] carry per-vulnerability discovery and release dates and dated remediations, including vendor fixes. GCVE [9] lets authorities publish under their own namespaces. BCP-05-X-03 [12] adds publishersupplied typed handling events. The subsequent BCP-05X-04 draft [13] specifies aggregated events with provenance and optional derived metrics; X-03 events can serve as inputs. Vulnerability-Lookup [6, 3] correlates these sources with KEV catalogs and typed sightings.

sections.title: 5 Data
sections.content: We measure on Vulnerability-Lookup instance as of 3 November 2026 (calculation time 2026-11-03T00:00Z), with the evidence model at Vulnerability-Lookup commit a9c6edf2. The instance holds the CVE corpus (418,263 records in its CVE 5 index), the advisories of 53 CSAF providers, national advisories (CERT-FR, CERTBund, NCSC-NL, CNVD, FSTEC), OSV and GitHub advisories, its KEV catalogs and its sightings, 97% of the exploited and proof-of-concept ones synchronised from the public instance  (Table 4)  . The exploited KEV entries come from Previdian (3,302 evidence records; the catalog was formerly named KEVIntel), CISA KEV (1,766), Shadowservers honeypot feed (1,283), the EU CSIRTs Network catalog published by ENISA (82), Anchor Identifiers Share exploitation disclosure public exploit patch discovery report, acknowledgement and 3,756 3,688 1,367 590 362 0 99.9% 98.1% 36.4% 15.7% 9.6% 0.0% 590 15.7% CIRCLs sinkhole (6) and two single entries. Exploited sightings include posts collected in real time from public and private Telegram channels and classified by local language model; each links to its post and can be verified by hand. Proof-of-concept sightings include the Exploit-DB entries (section 6.5). Population. We measure every identifier with exploitation evidence: an eligible KEV entry or an exploited sighting. There are 3,758 (3,690 of them CVEs). Each is passed through the same builder as the public timeline endpoint, read-only. For two identifiers the only exploitation evidence postdates the calculation time, so 3,756 have an exploitation anchor. The measurement script, the per-identifier output and its metadata are published with this paper.

sections.title: 6 Results
sections.content: 6.1 Coverage Disclosure is almost always dated, patches rarely, and the vendor-side dates VTEM needs never  (Table 5)  . No identifier with exploitation evidence carries report to its vendor or an acknowledgement, so VTEMs time to patch and vendor response time cannot be computed for any of them. The 362 discovery anchors are CSAF discovery date values, all but one Red Hats: the date the distributor learned of the vulnerability rather than its discovery. Only 590 identifiers (15.7%) have both an exploitation and patch anchor; 3,168 have no patch evidence at all, 3,166 of them with an exploitation anchor. Patch evidence is concentrated: of the 590 patch anchors, 323 are Red Hat and 209 Microsoft CSAF vendor fixes, 40 4 Table 6: Kind of date behind the exploitation anchor, over all identifiers and over those with patch anchor. Kind of date All With Catalog listing (KEV entry) First-hand observation (KEV entry) Classified channel post (sighting) Catalog listing (sighting) Other sightings Total 2,401 875 343 87 50 3, 475 22 81 1 11 590 come from the ENISA catalogs patchedSince and the rest from handful of sources. For most libraries the first recorded fix is distributors package, not the upstream release, which carries no dated record here. 6.2 What the exploitation dates are Table 6 classifies the exploitation anchors by the kind of date they carry. Catalog listings dominate: 2,401 anchors are the date KEV catalog listed the vulnerability, and 87 more are sightings mirroring such listing. First-hand observations, the first detection by honeypot or sinkhole, give 875 anchors, all but two from Shadowserver. Classified channel posts give 343. Catalogs also list in batches. On 19 days single catalog listed 25 or more vulnerabilities: CISA KEV listed 287 on 2021-11-03, its first day, and the import of Shadowservers history listed 324 on 2023-10-14. Imports into the instance do the same: on 12 days at least 25 entries of one catalog were recorded, 2,523 of Previdians on 2026-06-19. record date is an exploitation anchor only when the entry states no earlier date, 144 times here, all on such day. 1,041 exploitation anchors fall on listing or import batch day. They date the catalog, not the exploitation, which began earlier, often years earlier. 6.3 Exploitation to patch Of the 590 identifiers with both anchors, 135 have an exploitation anchor on batch day; we set them aside. Of the remaining 455, the order of the two dates is unknown for 89, because at least one is known only to the day and both fall on the same day. Patch evidence precedes the exploitation evidence for 307 (median 188.3 days, IQR 1544.4 to 28.4), and follows it for 59 (median 7.6 days, IQR 3.8 to 22.4; Table 7). The negative side mostly records vulnerability patched long before catalog listed it, not patch that preceded the first exploitation: the exploitation anchor is listing for most of these pairs. The positive side quantifies the gap between the recorded anchors. Of the 59 vulnerabilities with patch evidence after exploitation evidence, the patch anchor follows within day for 5, week for 27, and 30 days for 49; for 3 it follows after more than 90 days (at most 489 days). For 50 of them the exploitation anchor is catalog listing (median 7.2 days), for 5 first-hand observation (22.7 days), for 3 Metric Median IQR 7.6 Exploitation to patch, > 0 Exploitation to patch, < 0 Disclosure to exploit, > 0 2,389 Disclosure to exploit, < 0 69 Disclosure to patch, > 0 365 Total time to patch, > 0 332 Disclosure to public exploit, > 0 1,337 59 3.8 22.4 307 188.3 1544.4 28.4 27.6 1316.8 24.4 1.5 5.1 42.2 4.9 39.9 75.4 1593.0 298.0 4.3 13.3 11.4 610.0 classified channel post and for one another sighting; 42 of their patch anchors are Red Hat fixes. What the data supports is therefore narrower than time from exploitation to patch: it is mostly the time from catalog listing to the first recorded, frequently downstream, fix. 6.4 Other intervals Exploitation evidence follows public disclosure by median of 298 days when batch listings are set aside, and precedes it for 69 vulnerabilities (median 4.3 days before). Patch evidence follows disclosure by median of 13.3 days (365 identifiers), coincides at the recorded timestamp for 147, and precedes it for 13, 11 of them through ENISA patchedSince dates. The first published proof of concept follows disclosure by median of 610 days. It is the first proof of concept recorded here, an Exploit-DB publication or channel post; an exploit published elsewhere earlier leaves no dated trace in this data. 6.5 Effect of evidence classification The figures above were preceded by four corrections of the evidence, each visible only once every anchor could be traced to its record. In first measurement, on 28 October, 2,225 of 5,620 exploitation anchors (40%) were Exploit-DB entries: the collector feeding them stored each entry as an exploited sighting, dated with the publication of the exploit, following taxonomy revision that had no proof-of-concept value. An Exploit-DB entry is public exploit code, VTEMs exploit published. Once the entries were retyped as proofs of concept, the population fell from 5,620 to 3,574 identifiers, the identifiers exploited before disclosure from 458 to 86, and the median of patch evidence after exploitation from 39.5 to 10.6 days. Second, the first detections of Shadowservers honeypots tied with their listing date and were selected as reports; recognising first-hand evidence turned 949 anchors into observations, and flagging batch listings removed the catalog-launch dates from the intervals. Third, 375 of Previdians 3,302 entries (11%) date their listing with the CVE records publication instant, to the second, for vulnerabilities published from 2008 on: the catalog states no listing date for them. Read as listings, they more than doubled the vulnerabilities exploited before disclosure (157 instead of 69), most by fraction of second, and replaced honeypot first 5 detections by dates years earlier. Set aside, they leave the entrys record date, the day the instance imported the backlog, flagged as batch listing. Fourth, the instance had stored SUSEs copy of about 3,600 Red Hat advisories, which SUSE republishes under Red Hats identifiers, in place of Red Hats own. Restoring them made 49 patch anchors earlier and supplied 12; none moved later. Of the 79 identifiers whose patch evidence followed exploitation evidence in the 28 October run, 55 remain, 16 now fall on an import day and for 8 the patch evidence now comes first, 5 of them through the restored Red Hat fixes; the following weeks data adds 4. None of the corrections changed the arithmetic, yet each moved the figures.

sections.title: 7 Threats to Validity
sections.content: Exploitation dates are upper bounds at best. Every exploitation anchor is the date the evidence was produced, not the date exploitation began, and it bounds exploitation only if that date is accurate. 2,401 of 3,756 are catalog listings; only 875 are first detections by honeypot or sinkhole, and honeypot sees attempts against its own sensors, from the day it watches for them. Batch listings are flagged and set aside, and catalog date that is the publication instant to the second is not read as listing (section 6.5); placeholder date in any other form would go unnoticed. catalog that lists vulnerability few days after exploitation began is indistinguishable from one that lists it the same day. If its anchor is accurate, exploitation began no later than it, which can only shorten an interval that starts there; but the first recorded patch can be later than the first fix (below), which lengthens it. The two errors do not cancel in known direction, so an exploitationto-patch value is neither lower nor an upper bound on the true exposure. Selection. The population is what this instances catalogs and sightings recorded. KEV catalog lists what its maintainer observed and chose to publish, with its own scope; CISAs, for instance, is driven by the needs of US federal agencies. Vulnerability statistics inherit the selection biases of their databases [16]: the figures describe the evidence that is published and machine-readable, not the population of exploited vulnerabilities. Patch dates. The patch anchor is the first fix recorded on the instance. For most libraries it is distributors package (Red Hat) or vendor advisory (Microsoft); the upstream fix usually has no dated record, so the patch date can be months after the upstream release. The ENISA catalogs patchedSince dates are statements of CSIRT; for 11 vulnerabilities they precede disclosure, which suggests that some are approximate. fixs availability says nothing about its deployment. Patch evidence without date is not used. Records often say that fix exists, and which release carries it, without saying when it was released, for which the format has no field (section 2). Of the 3,168 identifiers without patch evidence, 821 (25.9%) have CVE or NVD reference tagged patch, 182 of them to commit or pull request. The version survey finds CNA version-status candidates for 795 (25.1%) and NVD range boundaries for 1,251 (39.5%), 1,503 (47.4%) in either. These are not verified fixes: unaffected versions may predate the flaw, and excluded bounds need not name released versions [7]. Dating them requires verifying the product, branch, release and fix. Only 88 of the 795 CNA records supply repo or collectionURL with packageName for lookup. tag is also not release, and two records from outside the population show the error in both directions: one, whose timeline has only fix-developed and whose reference is the commit, is reported unpatched although its named fixed version was released 20 days before disclosure; in the other, the reference tagged patch is commit in no release yet, fix no user can install. Patch coverage is therefore the coverage of dated fix evidence, not of fixes. Discovery dates. The only discovery dates in the population are CSAF discovery date values of distributors, which record when the distributor learned of the vulnerability: 192 of the 362 (53%) are later than the public disclosure, and 18 even follow the distributors own fix in the same advisory. Total time to patch therefore measures distributors awareness-to-fix time, not VTEMs discovery-to-patch time; such dates are flagged, and they do not start the lifecycle-wide metrics. Disclosure dates. disclosure date is documents date, and document covering several vulnerabilities need not have disclosed each of them on that date. Advisories gain vulnerabilities in later revisions, industrial-control advisories in particular, which are updated for years as the third-party components of product gain vulnerabilities. Before such revisions were recognised, 36 of 3,688 disclosure anchors (1%) were the release date of an advisory that added the vulnerability later; recognising the revisions moves them later by median of 14 days and up to 723. 2026 vulnerability was dated by 2024 advisory, and its disclosure-to-patch interval was 744 days instead of 21. Once the revision is recognised, the anchor of 32 of the 36 comes from an earlier record, the CVE record for 15: the revision was not the first disclosure either. Revisions are recognised by their wording (Added CVE-. . . , Ajout des identifiants. . . , . . . erganzt, or the identifiers named as new); an unrecognised one leaves the release date, which makes disclosure date early and an interval that starts there long. Exploitation to patch does not depend on disclosure. Classification. Sighting types are assigned by their collectors. One collectors choice, recording Exploit-DB entries as exploitation, made 40% of the exploitation anchors in our first measurement (section 6.5). Telegram sightings are classified by local language model; each can be verified against its post, but the classifiers precision on the sightings that become anchors (343 exploitation, and the proof-of-concept 6 ones) is unmeasured. Removing the 81 pairs anchored on channel post from the 455 outside batch days, without replacing their anchors, leaves the positive side almost unchanged (56, median 7.6 days, IQR 3.722.1) but moves the negative median from 188.3 to 127.7 days (229 pairs). proofof-concept sighting does not establish that the code works. Future work follows from these gaps: the precision of the channel-post classifier; dating fix evidence at import time, once candidate fixed version or fix commit is verified, from the first release that carries it; repeated measurements as publishers adopt timelines; and the roll-up by product and vendor that was VTEMs original purpose. 439 of Precision. the 590 exploitation/patch intervals (74.4%) have at least one endpoint known only to the day, bare date or timestamp at exactly midnight UTC. The bounds cover timestamp precision only, at most day in either direction; reporting delays and missing earlier evidence remain unbounded. The order of 89 pairs is unknown, reported apart. Snapshot and identity. The measurement reads one instance on one day. Feeds, catalogs and sightings change continuously: two identifiers gained their exploitation evidence on the day of the measurement, after the calculation time, and synchronisation of the KEV catalogs before the measurement added 595 entries, week of listings. Linked records count only when they state that they describe the vulnerability, which excludes records without such fields (some national databases) and errs towards fewer, safer inputs.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Open, machine-readable evidence is enough to compute, for each vulnerability, the interval between exploitation and patch, together with lifecycle intervals adapted from those VTEM named in 2015, and to trace every figure to the record that produced it, with its precision and the kind of evidence behind it. What it is not yet enough for is the claim the interval invites. Of 3,758 identifiers with exploitation evidence, 590 have patch evidence at all; most exploitation dates are catalog listings; the vendor-side dates VTEM needs are never published; and once catalog backlogs and unordered sameday pairs are set aside, 59 vulnerabilities remain whose patch evidence follows their exploitation evidence, by median of 7.6 days, mostly from catalog listing to distributors fix. Two results matter beyond the numbers. First, traceability is what made the data correctable: single collectors classification of exploit publications as exploitation moved 40% of the exploitation dates, and it was found because each anchor names its source; so were catalogs placeholder listing dates, which had moved quarter of the vulnerabilities whose patch followed their exploitation. Second, the gaps are specific and can be closed by publishers. Timelines in the records themselves (GCVE BCP-05-X-03: reported, acknowledged, fix available, exploitation observed) would supply the vendor-side dates; catalogs that publish first observation separately from their listing date would turn listing dates, upper bounds at best, into observations; and dated upstream fixes, fix-available event rather than an undated patch reference or fix-developed event alone, would remove the distributor lag from patch dates.

sections.title: Reproducibility and Artifacts
sections.content: Code: Vulnerability-Lookup [6] (github.com/vulnerability-lookup/vulnerability-lookup, AGPL-3.0). The evidence model is website/lib/ vulnerability_timeline.py, documented in docs/vulnerability-timeline.md. Pull request #714 (cadc9086) introduced it; #753 (first-hand observations, batch listings, catalog patch dates), #764 (origin), #765 and #768 (revisions adding vulnerability), #766 and #767 (copied publication times, import days) and #769 (Red Hat advisories in the SUSE feeds, with tools/fix_csaf_suse_redhat_copies.py) refined it. Every figure is computed at a9c6edf2. #752 added the retype sightings command of section 6.5. Collector: ExploitDBSighting (github.com/vulnerability-lookup/ExploitDBSighting), pull request #4 (Exploit-DB entries are proofs of concept) and commit 553eb0f (unverified entries imported). Per-vulnerability evidence: every Vulnerability-Lookup instance serves the events and durations of vulnerability, each with its source, record, field, precision and basis, at /api/vulnerability/{id}/timeline, for instance on vulnerability.circl.lu. Measurement: scripts/measure_coverage.py in the paper repository runs, read-only, inside Vulnerability-Lookup checkout, through the same builder as the endpoint above, and records the commit, the calculation time and the batch days. scripts/paper_figures.py derives every figure of sections 6 and 7 from its output, and observation_sensitivity.py details the source exclusions; scripts/instance_stats.py, patch_references.py and fixed_versions.py give those of section 5 and the undated patch evidence. Results: results/ holds the per-identifier output (anchors with source, record and field; durations with bounds, order and batch flags) of every run. Historical exports omit original date values, entry UUIDs and some diagnostic flags; new exports retain them. The figures of this paper are those of 7 coverage-2026-11-03-paper (a9c6edf2, calculation time 2026-11-03T00:00Z) and of the instance and survey files of that day; the comparisons use the same data with the model before #765 (-pre765). Earlier runs document the corrections of section 6.5, and NOTES.md records each run and the decisions between them. Data: the instance itself is not redistributed. Its sources are public (CVE records, CSAF providers, national advisories, KEV catalogs) or served by the public instance (sightings, KEV entries). run on another instance or another day will differ; the per-identifier output is what makes each figure here traceable.
